lawyer:
Md. Abdur Rouf with Sharifuddin Chaklader ------ for the Petitioner (in all the three Rules). 
Kaiseruddin Ahmed ------ for the Opposite Parties (In all the three Rules).
parties:
Ibrahim Hossain in C.R. No. 1176/76 and 1178/76. Delwara Begum in C.R No. 1179/76 ------Petitioners.
Vs.
Md. Khorshed Ali and ors ------ Opposite Party
full_judgment:
Civil Rules Nos. 1176 and 1178 of 1976 at the instance of the purchaser Md Ibrahim Hossain and Civil Rule No. 1176 of 1976 at the instance of purchaser Mst. Delwara Begum, wife of Md. Ibrahim Hossain were issued calling upon the opposite party No. 1 pre-emptor Md. Khorshed Ali to show cause, why the judgments and orders dated 6.5.76 passed by the learned Munsif 2nd Court, Mymensingh, Sadar, in the proceedings under Order 9 rule 13 of the Code of Civil Procedure arising out of orders, allowing pre-emption ex-parte under section 24 of the Non-Agricultural Tenancy Act, 1949, should not be set aside. These Rules are dis-posed of by this judgment. 

 2. One Md. Khorshed Ali as pre-emptor, on or about 20th December, 1973, filed applications for pre-emption under section 24 of the Non-Agricultural Tenancy Act 1949 against the purchaser Md. Ibrahim Hossain and Mst. Delwara Begum wife of Md. Ibrahim Hossain respectively for sales in question, by Mohini Chandra Tarafder by deeds executed on 14.8.73 and registered on 21.8.73. The applications were registered as Misc. Judl. Cases Nos. 865, 864 and 863 of 19'3 respectively. The 20th day of September, 1975 was the date fixed for pre-emptory hearing of these Misc. Jud. Cases under section 24 of the Act. On 18th September, 1975 applications for shifting the date of hearing by Md. Ibrahim Hossain for himself and fir his wife as her tadbircar were filed on the ground of illness. No medical certificate etc. was attached to the applications but the learned Munsif, however, being satisfied, adjourned the case till 25.9.75. On 25.9.75 an application at the instance of the learned Lawyer of the purchasers was filed to the effect that the case was fixed for hearing on 20th September, 1975 on which date the purchasers petitioners prayed for time on the ground of illness and the Court was pleased to grant time till 25.9.75 but that date being a date just on the eve of Annual Vacation„ the petitioners might reasonably assume that the next date would be fixed after the ensuing long vacation and that the petitioner might not expect so short adjournment for 5 days only till 25.9.75 just on the eve of the long vacation. It was also stated in the petition that since the petitioner was suffering from illness even from earlier date, he might not have recovered from his illness on that date; so the prayer for adjournment was made. The Court below rejected the application for adjournment and on 25.9.75 the cases were heard ex-party and pre-emption was allowed. On or about 1-10-75 the purchaser petitioner Md. Ibrahim Hossain filed two applications under Order 9, rule 13 read with section 151 of the Code of Civil Procedure which were registered as Miscellaneous Cases Nos. 1304 and 1297 of 1975 and the other purchaser Mst. Delwara Begum, wife of Md. Ibrahim Hossain filed another application under the same section which was also registered as Miscellaneous Case No 1303 of 1975, on the grounds, amongst other, that the petitioner was informed by the messenger that the prayer for shifting the date petition dated 18.9.75 has been allowed but he or she was not aware of the shifted date, 25.9.75, at all Moreover, Md. Ibrahim Hossain, the petitioner and tadbirker, was suffering from illness 3/4 days before the date of peremptory hearing of the original Misc. Judl. case and the petitioners have suffered irreparable loss by ex-parte order. 

 4. Ali these Misc. cases under Order 9, rule 13 of the Code of Civil Procedure were heard and dismissed on 26th May, 1976 mainly on the ground that application under Order 9 rule 13 C.P.C is not maintainable in a proceeding under section 24 of Non-Agricultural Tenancy Act and that the petitioners failed to prove the cases attempted to be made out in the petition. Hence the above Rules. 

 5. Mr. Md. Abdur Rouf, the learned Advocate in support of the Rules contended before me that the learned Court below failed to exercise its jurisdiction in deciding the scope of Order 9, rule 13 of the Code of Civil Procedure in a Proceeding under section 24 of the Non-Agricultural Tenancy Act and also mis-directed himself in exercising the jurisdiction by omitting to read the evidence and construing the same in its true perspective. 

 6. Mr. Kaiseruddin Ahmed, the learned Advocate opposed these Rules mainly on the ground that the orders datee 25.9.75 allowing the pre-emption ex-parte passed in the proceeding under section 24 of the Non-Agricultural Tenancy Act, being not a decree in suit, the application under Order 9, rule 13 C.P.C. for "setting aside ex-parte decree in a suit" is not maintainable. He also submits that assuming but not admitting the fact that the Order 9, rule 13 of the Code is applicable in that case the revision under section 115 of the Code of Civil Procedure is not maintainable as there is provision of appeal under Order 43, rule 1(4) of the Code of Civil Procedure. 

 7. The whole question is whether the application under Order 9, rule 13 C.P C. is applicable in a proceeding under section 24 of the Non-Agricultural Tenancy Act. If applicable, whether appeal will lie to this Court under 43 rule 1(d) C.P.C. or the revision is the appropriate remedy in the circumstances of the case. 

 9. Section 24(9) of the Non-Agricultural Tenancy Act provides—"An appeal from any order of a Court under this section shall lie to the Civil Appellate Court having jurisdiction to entertain such appeals." The petitioners have not availed of their statutory right of appeal against the aforesaid Ex-parte order dated 25.9.75. They have preferred applications under. Order 9, rule 13 of the C.P.C. for setting aside the above order. There are series of decisions that the procedure provided in the Code in regard to suits are applicable in all independent proceeding s of original nature, such as proceedings under the Provincial Insolvency Act, Guardian and Wards Act, Succession Act, Land Acquisition Act, Hindu Marriage Act, Arbitration Act, Rent Control Ordinance & Act and W.P. Urban Rent Restriction Ordinance etc. Non-Agricultural Tenancy Act does not specifically make the Code of Civil Procedure applicable to a case under section 24 of the Act. Section 4 of the Civil Procedure Code does not limit or otherwise affect any special Law. In other words, the provisions of the Code of Civil Procedure which run counter to the special or local law are excluded. This section does not bar the applicability of the Code where special or local law is silent. Section 141 of the Code of Civil Procedure runs as follows "The Procedure provided in this Code in regard to suits shall be followed, as far as it can be made applicable, in all proceedings in any Court of civil jurisdiction: In view of these provisions Mr. Rouf submits that the provisions of the Code of Civil Procedure subject to restrictions herein and subject to provisions of the Special Act, are applicable on all force in the present case and the provisions of Order 9, rule 13 C.P.C. is also equally applicable in these proceedings under section 24 of said Act even though it is not a suit. He first relied upon the case of Thakur Prasad-Vs. Sk. Fakirullah and another 23 Indian Appeals 44. In that case, the bar of bringing fresh suit in the event of the withdrawal of the first suit without leave of the Court to bring fresh suit as provided in sec. 373 (old) could riot create a bar, of course, on proper appreciation of the facts in an independent proceedings but for the procedure provided in section 647 (old).-141 (new) of the Code of Civil Procedure to follow as far as it can be made applicable in all proceedings in any Code of civil jurisdiction other than the suits and appeals. It has also been decided that section 647 (old), (new section 141) of the Code of Civil Procedure does not on its true construction prohibit an application for execution where a former application to that effect has been withdrawn without liberty to present a fresh one. In the case of Jamiyat Ali. Vs. Mrs. Chemon Ara Begum and others, (1968) 20 D L.R. (Dacca) 480 a Division Bench has held:— 

 "Proceeding under section 96 of the State Acquisition Act being original in nature, the procedure provided in the Code of Civil Procedure, in view of section 141 of the Code is applicable, as far as it can be.'' 

 10. Keeping in view the above principles, certain decisions may be cited for our purpose, relating to the proceedings under section 174 of Bengal Tenancy Act. Order 21, rule 90 C.P.C., section 96 of the State Acq. Act, s. 26-F of the Bengal Tenancy Act and s. 24 of the Non-Agricultural Tenancy Act. In the case of Munsur Ahmed VS. Dakshina Chandra Sen and others, (1959) 11 DLR (Dac) 449 ; P.L.D. 1960 (Dacca) 130, Chowdhury, J. held : 

 "Therefore, in any view of the matter, an application under section 173(3) or the Bengal Tenancy Act is an application under the special provision of the Bengal Tenancy Act and it is an independent proceeding and not an execution proceeding and the provisions of Order IX rule 9 read with section 141 of the Code of Civil Procedure, are applicable to such an application." 

 "If it is an independent proceeding in the nature of original proceeding that Shall by operation of section 141 of the Code of Civil Procedure attract the provision of Order IX, rule 13, C.P.C., with the result that the order complained of shall prevail as sound and legal.'' In the case of Birendra Nath Biswas Vs. Monorarna Devi and others, reported in A.I.R. 1948 Cal. 77, Harries C J. in course of pre-emption proceeding under section 26-F of the Bengal Tenancy Act, held : 

 "Order 9 r. 9. in terms is confined to suits and on the face of it the order would have no application to a proceeding under S. 26F of the Bengal Tenancy Act, as such proceeding is not a suit. Section 141 of the Code, however, provides: The procedure provided in this Code in regard to suits shall be followed, as far as it can be made applicable, in all proceedings in a Court of Civil Jurisdiction. That being so, the procedure laid down by 0. 9, r. 9 though in terms applicable only to suits is also applicable to applications in a civil. Court by reason of S.141". 

 11. In an unreported case of Mohammad Ali Vs. Dr. M. Abdul Giffur and others in Civil Revision Case No. 652/67. Abdulla, J. in a proceeding under section 96 of the East Pakistan State Acquisition and Tenancy Act relying upon the above 22 Indian Appeal, 44 has held: 

 So Order IX rule 13 C.P.C. is applicable in the present proceeding. Mr. Kaiseruddin Ahmed, learned Advocate appearing on behalf of the opposite party No. I strenuously argued that the learned Munsif is right in holding that provision of Order 9, rule 13 C.P.C. is not applicable in pre-emption proceeding under section 24 of the Non-Agricultural Tenancy Act. Reliance has been made both by the learned Munsif as well as by the learned Advocate to the case of Haji Rahimuddin Sheikh and another Vs. Nasirnaddi Sheikh, 53 C.W.N. (Cal) I.D.R. 62 where in Akrarn C. J. in connection with a proceeding under section 26F of the Bengal Tenancy Act interpreting section 141 of the Code of Civil Procedure held that no appeal lies in the Civil Procedure Code against an order dismissing an application under Order 9 rule 13 C.P.C. for restoring a proceeding under section 26F of the Bengal Tenancy Act which had been disposed of ex-parte. He also relied upon the case of Seferaddi Munshi Vs. Farman Ali Mirdha & another reported in 4 D.L.R. 621 wherein a similar question arose in connection with the proceeding under section 26F of the B.T. Act as to whether an appeal lies when an application under Order Q, rule 13 C.P.C. for setting aside an ex-pane order is dismissed and Ibrahim, J. ; held : —"The right of appeal allowed by order 43 rule 1(d) Code of Civil procedure is limited only to an order rejecting an application for an order to set aside a decree passed ex-parte. What is essential is that the application under Order 9, rule 13, must be an application for an order to set aside an ex-parte decree if it is an application to Set aside an ex-parte order, as in this case, an order rejecting the application does not become appealable under this clause." The next case relied upon is the case of Kafiluddin Chowdhury Vs. Dr. Abdus Sattar ported in 20 D.L.R (Dacca) 1220, where in connection with a proceeding under section 24 of the Non-Agricultural Tenancy Act while referring the scope of section 141 C P.C. it has been decided by a Division Bench that the provision made therein is in regard to procedural matter. It does not create any sub-stantive right such as right of appeal which is conferred by a Law. It was further held that Order 9 rule 9 of the Code of Civil Procedure provides that there may b an application for restoration of a suit dismissed for default. This is a procedural matter and as such this rule cannot have the effect of conferring a substantive right of appeal. Another Division Bench in C.R. No. 1305 of 1974 in a proceeding under section 96 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act held the same view. It appears that the appeal baying been provided in the main Special Act and section 141 C.P.C. being confined to the suits and proceedings only, the right of appeal against an order under Order 9 rule 9 C.PC cannot be availed of. So the contention of the learned Advocate for the opposite party to the effect that the Provisions of Order 9 rule 13 C.P.C. is not applicable in the proceeding like the present one, firstly because it is not for setting aside a decree and secondly, because since there is no provision of appeal against an order under Order 9 rule 13 C.P.C. in this proceeding under section 24 of the said Act, in spite of the provisions of S. 141 C.P.C. is not tenable in law. 

 13. The next question is to see whether the learned Munsif is right in holding that the purchasers petitioners had no reasonable ground for not making any appearance on the date fixed on 25.9.75 and thus have failed to prove their cases. It is apparent from his decision and from the records of the cases that he is wrong on the point as well. He believed even without medical certificate that there is a ground for adjournment of the case on 20.9.75 and, in fact, he adjourned the case till 25.9.75 Therefore, subsequently its bona fides that he was suffering from before 3/4 days of the hearing cannot be doubted. Then the question arises when the date of hearing was shifted from 20.9.75 to 25.9.75 on which date the case was disposed of ex-parte and whether the petitioner was in a position to know of that date of hearing on 25.9.75. It is abundantly clear from the evidence and also from the order of the learned Munsif that the lawyer's clerk did not inform the petitioner about the hearing date of 25.9.75. More so, when it appears from the record that on 25.9.75 it is the learned lawyer who filed an application for shifting on the ground mentioned above and not the petitioner himself. The petitioners got the information from the messenger that the prayer for shifting date has been allowed on the application dated 18.9.75, but neither the messenger nor the witnesses including P.W. 2 has said about the date of 25.9.75 till which date the case were shifted, to the petitioners. The evidences of P.Ws. 2 and 3 have been misread and misconstrued or omitted to read the same. Moreover, that the impugned orders were passed on the eve of the annual vacation of the Civil Court are not disputed at all. It is also the case made out in the petition that the petitioners might not have expected the adjournment of the cases for so short time on the eve of the vacation. All these facts have been established by the petitioners but still then it resulted in the order of ex-parte dismissal of the Misc. Judi. cases under section 24 of the Non-Agricultural Tenancy Act adverse to the interest of the petitioners. 

 In the result, all these rules are made absolute and the Miscellaneous cases tinder section 24 of the Non-Agricultural Tenancy Act are hereby restored but the petitioners must be liable to ply costs both of these proceedings as well as proceedings under Order 9, rule 13 C.P.C. in the Court below which collectively with the consent by both the learned Advocates, has been assessed at Tk. 250/- in each case payable by the purchasers petitioners to the pre-emptor opposite party No. 1. The cases before the Court below should be disposed of as expeditiously as possible. Let the records be sent down immediately.
